opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot. The short version is that when you see what looks like a sudden, sharp jump in capability as you scale a model, you should first ask how much of that jump comes from the model and how much comes from the yardstick you're using to measure it.

A lot of the early emergence claims relied on metrics that are nonlinear or discontinuous in the model's underlying per-token performance. Exact match is the classic example. Say you're asking a model to do multi-digit addition and you only give credit if every digit is right. As the model improves smoothly at predicting each token, the probability of getting the whole string right can look like it's sitting near zero for a long time and then shoots up. That curve looks dramatic, but it may be a fairly predictable consequence of compounding per-token accuracy rather than some qualitative phase change inside the model.

So in our work we did a few things. We took the same model outputs and re-scored them with continuous or linear metrics, like token edit distance or Brier score, and a lot of the sharp transitions became smooth, predictable trends. We also went the other direction. We took vision models, where nobody was really claiming emergence, picked metrics deliberately designed to be harsh, and we could induce what looked like emergent behavior. That's a pretty strong signal that the metric is doing a lot of the work.

There's also a resolution issue. If you only evaluate on a small test set, you can't distinguish "zero" from "very small but nonzero." So part of what looks like nothing-then-something is really you not having enough samples to see the gradual improvement.

In terms of what researchers should actually do, I'd say a few things. First, report multiple metrics, including at least one that's continuous with respect to the model's outputs, and check whether the effect survives. Second, think about statistical resolution: make sure your eval is big enough to detect small changes, and put error bars on things. Third, be explicit about what claim you're making. "The model's behavior on this metric changes sharply" is a different claim from "the model has acquired a new capability at some scale," and we tend to slide from one to the other.

And I want to be careful here, because people sometimes read our work as "emergence doesn't exist." That's not the claim. The point is that metric choice can create the appearance of emergence, so the burden is on us to rule that out before we attribute it to the model. It's also true that sometimes the harsh metric is the one you care about. If you're deploying a system and only fully correct answers matter, then a sharp transition in exact match is practically real for you. You just shouldn't conclude from that alone that something fundamentally new is happening inside the model. Keeping those two questions separate, what matters for downstream use versus what's happening mechanistically, would clear up a lot of the confusion in this debate.

r001.rationale: The response says claims should specify whether behavior changes sharply on a particular metric or whether the model acquired a capability, and recommends checking multiple metrics.

r002.rationale: The response says continuous or linear metrics that give partial credit make sharp transitions smoother; it attributes sharper behavior to harsh metrics such as exact match.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the core observation in our work is that a lot of what gets called emergence is really an artifact of how we measure. If you take a metric like exact-match accuracy, you're applying a very nonlinear, all-or-nothing transformation to the model's underlying behavior. A model that gets nine out of ten tokens right in a multi-step problem scores exactly the same as one that gets zero right. So as scale increases and per-token performance improves smoothly, the aggregate metric sits near zero for a long time and then suddenly jumps. That looks like a phase transition, but the underlying capability was improving continuously the whole time.

So the first thing I'd say to researchers is: before you claim a capability emerges, ask what the metric is doing to the signal. If you swap exact match for something continuous, like token-level edit distance or per-token log-likelihood, and the sharp curve becomes smooth and predictable, then the emergence was in your measurement, not in the model.

The second thing is about statistical resolution. Many of these benchmarks have a few hundred examples, and small models sit near zero accuracy. At that regime you have almost no resolution to detect small improvements. When we increased the test set size, apparent discontinuities often smoothed out because we could actually see the gradual climb from the floor.

And the third point, which I think gets lost, is that we're not saying scale doesn't matter or that nothing interesting happens with scale. Clearly capabilities improve. What we're pushing back on is the claim that these changes are fundamentally unpredictable or sharp in some deep way. That claim has real consequences for how people think about safety, forecasting, and governance. If you believe capabilities appear out of nowhere, you plan very differently than if you believe they follow smooth, extrapolable trends under the right metric.

So concretely, I'd want researchers to report results under multiple metrics, especially continuous ones, to be explicit about the resolution of their evaluation, and to treat emergence as a hypothesis that needs to survive those controls rather than as the default explanation whenever a curve bends.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should examine what a metric does before claiming emergence and recommends treating emergence as a hypothesis that must survive metric controls.

r002.rationale: The response says continuous metrics such as edit distance or log-likelihood can make a sharp curve smooth; it does not say partial-credit metrics make behavior sharper.

astra-6.text:
I think the metric has to be part of the claim. When we say an ability emerges, we’re usually saying that some measured performance changes sharply as we scale the model. But that sharp change can come from the way we measure performance, rather than a sharp change in the model itself.

For example, if you score an answer as correct only when the entire string matches, the model might be improving steadily on individual tokens while getting zero credit. Then suddenly it starts producing complete correct answers, and the curve looks like a jump. A more graded measure might reveal that underlying progress.

So I’d want researchers to examine several reasonable metrics, explain why each is relevant to the task, and check how sensitive the conclusion is to those choices. That doesn’t mean an exact-match metric is wrong—sometimes getting the whole answer right is precisely what matters. But an abrupt change in task success is a narrower claim than saying the model suddenly acquired a fundamentally new capability. We should be clear about which claim the evidence supports.

r001.rationale: It says the metric must be part of the emergence claim and asks researchers to explain and test sensitivity to metric choices.

r002.rationale: It says a graded measure may reveal steady underlying progress, rather than stating that partial-credit metrics are expected to show sharper behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that emergence is a claim about both the model and how we measure it. If you use a metric like exact match, you get no credit until the entire answer is correct. So the model could be improving gradually, but the metric makes that improvement look like a sudden jump.

That doesn’t mean the jump is irrelevant. If your application requires an exactly correct answer, that threshold matters. But it’s a different claim from saying the model suddenly acquired a fundamentally new capability.

So I’d want researchers to check how sensitive the result is to the metric. Does the same pattern show up if you give partial credit or look at the probability assigned to the correct answer? And how much uncertainty is there, particularly when performance is close to zero? If the apparent emergence disappears under another reasonable measure, then the claim should reflect that. We observed a sharp change under this particular evaluation, rather than established that the underlying capability appeared discontinuously.

r001.rationale: The response says emergence claims depend on the metric and recommends qualifying claims when a sharp change appears only under a particular evaluation.

r002.rationale: It suggests checking whether the pattern persists with partial credit, but does not state that sharper behavior is expected with partial-credit metrics.
